lesson.title: Reading the Titration Curve
lesson.summary: A titration curve plots the analyte's pH against the volume of titrant added, and its distinctive S-shape, especially the steep jump near the middle, is how chemists visualize exactly when a titration reaction is complete.
lesson.body:
A titration is not just a single endpoint moment, it is a continuous process, and plotting that process reveals a lot more than the endpoint alone. A titration curve graphs pH on the vertical axis against volume of titrant added on the horizontal axis, using the same graphing skills you would apply to any other set of paired data: each addition of titrant, paced out in small measured volumes, gives one more pH reading and one more point on the curve.

For a strong acid titrated with a strong base, or the reverse, the curve has a recognizable S-shape. At the start, pH changes slowly as titrant is added, because there is a large excess of unreacted analyte buffering the change. As the analyte gets closer to being fully consumed, the curve suddenly turns steep, and a very small addition of titrant, sometimes a single drop, causes a large jump in pH. After that steep region, the curve flattens out again as the solution becomes dominated by excess titrant.

Weak acid and weak base titrations produce curves with the same overall S-shape but with important differences. The initial pH is less extreme, since a weak acid does not ionize completely. A region appears where the pH changes only gradually even as titrant continues to be added, because the weak acid and its conjugate base together resist pH change, and the final flat region sits on the opposite side of pH 7 from where a strong acid and strong base titration would land. The details of exactly why that buffering region resists change are explored further once acid-base equilibrium is covered, but the shape difference on the graph is something you can already recognize.

Applying this to the HCl and NaOH titration from the previous chapter, the curve for that experiment would start at a low pH, since 20.00 mL of 0.0750 M HCl is a fairly acidic solution, then rise gradually as NaOH is added, then jump steeply right around 15.00 mL, the same volume calculated earlier as the point where moles of NaOH added equal moles of HCl originally present. That steep, near-vertical section of the curve is not decorative, it marks the single most important point on the entire graph, and identifying it precisely is exactly the job of the equivalence point, discussed next.
